nameStory: The "tick-trefoil" name comes from this plant's notorious hitchhiking seeds that stick to clothing and fur like ticks, combined with its three-leaflet leaves (trefoil means "three leaves"). The "tall" part distinguishes it from its shorter relatives, as this species can reach impressive heights in good growing conditions.
description: Tall tick-trefoil is a sturdy wildflower that belongs to the legume family, the same group as beans and peas. This upright plant can grow 3-6 feet tall, with compound leaves made up of three oval leaflets. In late summer, it produces clusters of small pink to purple pea-like flowers along tall spikes, followed by segmented seed pods that break apart into sticky sections.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three oval leaflets per leaf, each 2-4 inches long with smooth edges and a somewhat leathery feel. The leaflets are relatively hairless (glabrous) and have a distinctive bluish-green color.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple flowers arranged in long, narrow clusters (racemes) at the top of the plant. Each flower is pea-like with the classic legume shape - about 1/4 inch long.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, jointed seed pods that break into triangular segments, each covered with tiny hooked hairs that grab onto fabric and fur with surprising tenacity.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, erect stems that can reach 6 feet, often growing in colonies from spreading roots. The main stem feels sturdy and somewhat woody at the base.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, green to reddish stems that are mostly hairless (matching the "glabellum" in its scientific name, which means "somewhat smooth").

habitat: Look for tall tick-trefoil in open woodlands, forest edges, and clearings with partial shade to full sun. It prefers well-drained soils and is often found along woodland paths, old fields transitioning back to forest, and disturbed areas where trees have been cleared.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as distinctive three-part leaves unfurl from the ground. Young plants are much shorter and easily overlooked among other spring vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August, with tall flower spikes making the plant most noticeable. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and become incredibly sticky - you'll know you've walked through tick-trefoil habitat when triangular seed pods cover your pants legs. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Only dried brown stems remain standing, sometimes with a few persistent seed pods still clinging to the stalks.

funFact: The hooked hairs on tick-trefoil seeds are so effective that they inspired part of the invention of Velcro - nature's original hook-and-loop fastener that can grab onto clothing from just a light brush against the plant!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tick-trefoils, especially showy tick-trefoil which has larger, showier flower clusters. Remember: tall tick-trefoil has smooth, bluish-green leaflets and narrow flower spikes, while showy tick-trefoil has hairy leaflets and dense, broader flower clusters.
contextualKnowledge: Also known as Dillenius' tick-trefoil after Johann Dillenius, an 18th-century German-British botanist. The scientific name "glabellum" means "somewhat smooth," referring to its relatively hairless leaves and stems compared to many of its fuzzy relatives.
compareHints: Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance. While showy tick-trefoil has broader, more densely packed flower clusters and hairy stems, tall tick-trefoil keeps things sleek with narrow flower spikes and smooth, bluish-green foliage. The round-leaved trailing species sprawls along the ground rather than standing tall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
